catalog_quote: There is no feature such as tenseness, nasal or stress in Biao. [sec. 2.3.1, p.50] ... Biao has a system of 6 tones in smooth syllables, i.e. syllables ending in vowels or nasal consonants -m, -n, -ŋ, including high level 55, dipping 214, high fall 53, low rise-fall 132, rise 35 and low level 22. There are 4 tones in checked syllables ... [sec. 2.6, p.55] ... Tone sandhi can be found in Biao. When syllables which combine with high pitch tones such as Tone 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 precede other syllables, the high pitch tones change to mid level pitch 33. When syllables which combine with low pitch tones, including Tone 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, precede other syllables, these low pitch tones become mid-low fall pitch 21. [p.57] ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Biao (10 lexical tones: 6 smooth + 4 checked) has no contrastive/phonemic stress; the only prominence remarks are morphological: in affixed words the root morpheme carries the stress and the few genuine prefixes (a55, to214, lak12) are unstressed 'minor' syllables (sesquisyllabic pattern). Tone sandhi (Lin 2009 for Yonggu; Liang 2024 sec. 2.6 for Shidong) neutralises non-final syllables (55 -> 33, other tones -> 21) while the final syllable keeps its citation tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Chinese loanwords generally do not undergo the tone sandhi (Lin 2009 sec. 2.2.5). No stress exceptions discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, impressionistic; no acoustic study. The p.50 sentence sits in the vowel (monophthong) section and may be read as 'no stressed/tense/nasal vowel features'; the root-stress / unstressed-prefix remarks are in the morphology chapter. The author's own data are Shidong Biao; Yonggu is covered only via the sec. 2.9 comparison (after Liang & Zhang 2002) and the explicit claim that the three areas share almost the same sound system. The Yonggu-specific phonology (Lin 2009) is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Liang Jingui 2024) is based on fieldwork in Shidong Township (Shidong Biao, biao1253) and describes 'Biao' as a single language, treating Yonggu (yong1283) as a 'vernacular area' with an almost identical sound system (sec. 2.9, after Liang & Zhang 2002); it is the same source and the same statement already used for biao1253, so a catalog entry for yong1283 would inherit it rather than rest on Yonggu-specific data. Glottolog (following Hsiu 2013) splits Biao into Shidong Biao [byk], Yonggu Biao and Dagang-Baoshan-Liangcun as mutually unintelligible languages; Chinese sources (Liang & Zhang 2002, Yang 2023, Liang 2024) treat them as dialects/vernaculars of one language, with Shidong + Yonggu forming the southern dialect. The only Yonggu-specific phonology (Lin Lunlun 2009, Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description for yong1283, held by the project) is silent on stress.

sources.note: Fieldwork on Shidong Biao but scoped as 'Biao' with Yonggu a 'vernacular area' whose sound system is 'almost the same' (sec. 2.9 p.68, Yonggu tone values tabulated after Liang & Zhang 2002). Sec. 2.3.1 p.50: 'There is no feature such as tenseness, nasal or stress in Biao.' Sec. 2.6: 10 tones + sandhi. Sec. 3.4 p.76: affixable morphemes 'are slight sounds, with the stress on the root morphemes'; p.81 prefix a55 'is unstressed'; p.83 to214/lak12/a55 unstressed, half a metrical foot (sesquisyllable).

sources.note: Nothing. Full Yonggu phonology (23 initials, 79 finals, 6 smooth + 4 checked tones: 55, 21, 43, 3253, 232, 52; 5, 232, 22, 342). Sec. 2.2 point 5: simple tone sandhi -- the preceding (non-final) syllable changes (high level 55 -> 33, other tones -> low falling 21), the final syllable normally keeps its tone; Chinese loans mostly exempt. No mention of 重音/轻声/word stress.
